decision.explanation: Expanding the numerator gives x^4-2x^2. For x≠0, the quotient equals x^2-2, whose limit as x→0 is -2.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1]}^{′}}{{[{x}^{2}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4x({x}^{2}-1)}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4{x}^{3}-4x}{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4{x}^{3}-4x}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[4{x}^{3}-4x]^{′}}{[2x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{12{x}^{2}-4}{2} \\  & =\frac{12(0)^{2}-4}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4}{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If we plug in x=0 we get the indeterminate form 00, so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

limx→0(x2−1)2−1x2=limx→0[(x2−1)2−1]′[x2]′=limx→04x(x2−1)2x=limx→04x3−4x2x

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form 00. To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

limx→0(x2−1)2−1x2=limx→04x3−4x2x=limx→0[4x3−4x]′[2x]′=limx→012x2−42=12(0)2−42=−42=−2.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{x}-x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{x}^{2}]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}-x-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{{e}^{x}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{x-1+{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{{e}^{x}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[2x]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Applying L'Hopital's rule gives lim(x→∞) √x/(4 ln x). Applying it again gives lim(x→∞) √x/8 = ∞.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{4}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are limx→∞x=∞ and limx→∞ln2⁡x=∞, respectively, so we have the case ∞∞.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

limx→∞xln2⁡x=limx→∞[x]′[ln2⁡x]′=limx→∞(12x)(2ln⁡xx)=limx→∞x4xln⁡x=limx→∞x4ln⁡x.

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form ∞∞. To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get limx→∞xln2⁡x=limx→∞x4ln⁡x=limx→∞[x]′[4ln⁡x]′=limx→∞(12x)(4x)=limx→∞x8x=18limx→∞x=∞.

limx→∞2x+9x−13x+5=

decision.explanation: Dividing numerator and denominator by x gives (2/√x+9−1/x)/(3+5/x), which tends to 9/3=3.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2\sqrt{x}+9x-1}{3x+5} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[2\sqrt{x}+9x-1]^{′}}{[3x+5]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}+9)}{3} \\  & =\frac{0+9}{3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Evaluate the following limit:
limx→0+cot⁡xecot⁡x=
Submit

decision.explanation: As x→0⁺, cot(x)→∞. Setting t=cot(x), L'Hopital's rule gives lim(t→∞) t/e^t = lim(t→∞) 1/e^t = 0.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]}^{′}}{{[{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{-{csc}^{2}⁡x}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{-{csc}^{2}⁡x}}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}\cancel{(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{{e}^{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
